To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
ABO blood group O and Rh+ blood group are the most frequent in seropositive and seronegative H. pylori patients.
the frequency of ABO blood group O is higher in H. pylor seropositive than seronegative symptomatic patients.

the frequencies of the O and Rh-positive blood groups were higher among seropositives than seronegatives, and that the frequencies of blood groups B and Rh-negative (Rh-) were higher among seronegatives than seropositives.

the association between H. pylori and ABO blood groups.
the association of the ABO blood groups with H. pylori and its relation to the development of peptic ulcer disease.
the association between the ABO and Rhs blood groups and seropositivity of H. pylori in patients suffering from dyspepsia in Erbil city, Iraq.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ABO blood groups do not play an important role in the development of H. pylori infections.
the O blood group is the most common blood group in seropositive H. pylori patients.
there is no association between ABO blood group phenotype and H. pylori status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the frequency of the O blood groups is high among seropositives, but it is low among seronegatives, and the frequency of the Rh+ blood group is high in both seropositives (92.5%) (p < 0.001) and seronegative groups (92.5%).
there is no relation between ABO blood group and Rh+ and H. pylori in symptomatic patients.
there is an association between the O blood group with seropositivity to H. pylori in patients with dyspeptic symptoms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ABO blood group is an independent risk factor associated with H. pylori infections in the Iraqi population.
H. pylori infections are not related to the Rh blood group.
H. pylori is more prevalent among the O blood group than other blood groups.
